title: Experimental Teaching System for Bone-Conducted Speech Enhancement and Edge-Deployable Speech Intelligence
content: Speech interfaces are becoming ubiquitous in medical and industrial devices, yet undergraduate laboratory teaching of speech signal processing still works almost exclusively on air-conducted recordings and supervised pipelines, ignoring both the physiology of alternative sensing channels and the data scarcity that dominates real deployments. This paper reports the design of an experimental teaching system that converts an active bone-conducted speech research programme, centred on a pre-trained Transformer with low-rank driven sparsity bootstrapping (TransLRC), into a four-tier undergraduate laboratory curriculum with an engineering layer. Four principles govern the design: constructive alignment, experiential progression, the research-teaching nexus, and the CDIO lifecycle. Each tier is anchored to a bottleneck that is genuinely open in the source research: characterising the body-channel distortion of bone-conducted speech, pre-training spectral representations without paired data, pruning attention through low-rank structure, and evaluating generalisation to unseen speakers under real-time budgets. Thirty-two laboratory units (64 contact hours) are organised into six modules with staged delivery and criterion-referenced assessment that admits documented negative results, mirroring the source study’s finding that pre-training and low-rank constraints contribute separable, measurable gains. Because the source protocol runs end-to-end on a single consumer GPU with a low-cost bone-conduction sensor, the curriculum targets faithful reproduction rather than scale-reduced approximation, giving students an unusually direct path from published result to reproduced result.
